nameStory: Sweet spurge earned its name because it's surprisingly mild compared to its relatives. While most spurges have an intensely bitter, caustic milky sap that burns the mouth and skin, this species is relatively gentle - hence the 'sweet' in its name, though you still shouldn't taste it!
description: Sweet spurge is a compact perennial herb that forms neat clumps in gardens and naturalized areas. This European native typically grows 1-2 feet tall with upright stems and small, inconspicuous flowers surrounded by colorful bracts. The most commonly seen form has deep purple foliage that creates striking contrast in shade gardens, though the original wild type has green leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow-green flowers lack true petals but are surrounded by small, leaf-like bracts that may be tinged with red or purple, clustered at stem tips in late spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to oblong leaves arranged alternately along stems, often with a purplish tint especially in the popular 'Chameleon' variety, feeling smooth and somewhat succulent to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading clumps 12-24 inches tall and wide, with multiple upright stems emerging from the base in a mounded shape

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Broken stems release a milky white sap that's less caustic than other spurges but should still be avoided on skin - wipe hands after handling

habitat: Sweet spurge thrives in partially shaded areas with moist, well-drained soil, often found in cultivated gardens, woodland edges, and disturbed areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers rich, organic soils and tolerates a range of moisture conditions from slightly dry to consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with distinctive purple-tinged foliage, followed by small clustered flowers in late spring that are more noticeable for their colorful bracts than the tiny blooms themselves.
seasonality.summer: Foliage remains attractive through summer, with purple-leaved varieties maintaining their color best in partial shade, while flowers fade and small three-chambered seed capsules develop.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may intensify in color before dying back, and mature seed capsules split open with a small popping sound to scatter seeds several feet away.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground parts visible until spring emergence.

funFact: Sweet spurge's seed capsules are like tiny biological cannons - when ripe, they explosively split open and can shoot seeds up to 15 feet away with an audible 'pop' that you can actually hear on quiet days!
confusionNotes: The purple-leaved garden variety might be confused with other purple-foliaged plants, but the distinctive milky sap when stems are broken is a dead giveaway. Remember: 'Spurge sap = milky white' - no other common garden plants have this characteristic.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'sweet,' this plant should never be eaten or allowed to contact eyes or open wounds. The common garden variety 'Chameleon' is actually much more purple than the original wild European form, which has plain green leaves.
compareHints: Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves. Most of its spurge relatives are either low, mat-forming plants with tiny leaves (like spotted spurge) or tall, narrow-leaved species (like cypress spurge). The purple foliage form is unmistakable when present.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
